thread: Follow food from the diversity of seeds into the tools and buildings of a working farm, then into the microscopic communities that transform a harvest. The swarm can become roots and grains, harvesters and kitchen implements, and finally the yeasts and bacteria of fermentation.

candidates.name: CGIAR Genebanks
candidates.why: Crop pages range from taro and yam to chickpea and finger millet, while genebank and resource sections reveal seed collections, germplasm health, and the work of keeping diverse crops alive.

candidates.name: The Food Museum
candidates.why: Historic farm buildings, baking equipment, dairy tools, recipes and a large object collection offer a lively passage from fieldwork to the kitchen.

candidates.name: University of Copenhagen Department of Food Science
candidates.why: Food research moves the journey into fermentation: yeasts, moulds, bacteria and phages interact with ingredients and equipment to make new flavors and preserve food.

candidates.name: The Museum of English Rural Life
candidates.why: Farm machinery, hand tools, livestock imagery and rural archives give the swarm wheels, working limbs and an abundance of farming characters.

candidates.name: Pasto Agricultural Museum
candidates.why: Sickles, plows, beekeeping equipment, ice-harvesting tools and old kitchen implements trace the work of cultivating and preserving food before electrification.

candidates.name: National Agriculture and Food Research Organization
candidates.why: Japan's agricultural research organization links a genebank of rice, beans and fruit to crop science, agricultural machinery, food research and field robotics.

candidates.name: Crop Trust
candidates.why: Crop diversity projects, seed vaults and genebank stories introduce wild relatives, stored seeds and the people and procedures that safeguard them.

candidates.name: Deutsches Museum
candidates.why: Its agriculture and food exhibition brings together a Lanz Bulldog tractor, a field robot, a combine harvester, brewing kettles and a steam oven.
